title: How peptides fold and assemble on surfaces
teaser: Sequence decides which residues anchor, which structure survives adsorption and whether neighbours order into layers.
summary: When a peptide meets a solid surface, its sequence decides almost everything: which side chains anchor, which secondary structure survives adsorption, and whether neighbouring chains order into layers. We compute conformational ensembles and free energies of peptides on graphite, gold and silver to learn those rules, and use them to choose sequences that fold, assemble or stabilize a nanoparticle on a given material.

title: What makes a nanoparticle choose a membrane
teaser: The lipid coat of a hybrid nanoparticle sets which membranes it binds, and mimicking the target is not the whole story.
summary: Wrapping a polymer core in lipids changes which cells a nanoparticle binds. We model hybrid lipid-polymer nanoparticles together with their target membranes to find what sets that selectivity; our recent work shows that lipid composition determines it, beyond simply mimicking the target membrane. Current theses extend this to the predictive design of lipid coatings, uptake by macrophages and photocontrollable carriers for colorectal cancer.
alt: Render of a coated nanoparticle embedded in a layer of molecules.

title: Surfaces that capture ions
teaser: Cyclic peptides grafted to a nanosurface as selective binding sites for ionic pollutants.
summary: A surface decorated with the right molecule can pull a specific ion out of water. We design cyclic peptides grafted to nanosurfaces as binding sites for ionic pollutants, and nanomaterials that capture and release ions selectively for mining processes and remediation. The question in every case is thermodynamic: how strongly, and how selectively, the site binds its ion in the presence of everything else in solution.
alt: Close-up render of peptide chains lying on a flat surface with small ions above them.

title: Ion channels, lipids and peptide materials
teaser: Simulations alongside experiments on channel regulation, membrane-active peptides and peptide hydrogels.
summary: Much of our work runs alongside experimental groups. Together we have described a peripheral PIP2-binding site that regulates TRP channels, the temperature dependence of charybdotoxin binding to Shaker K+ channels, and the electrostatic bridges that drive crosslinking of collagen-like peptides, and we have contributed simulations to peptide hydrogels for tissue repair. A current thesis studies how hydrophobic and cationic residues cooperate in antimicrobial peptides at lipid membranes.
